A.explanation: Too small to lower the density from $1.3$ to $1.1$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$ when starting with $40$ $\text{cm}^{3}$ of glycerine.

B.explanation: Gives total mass $60$ g in $48$ $\text{cm}^{3}$, so density $1.25$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$, still close to glycerine.

C.explanation: Gives total mass $86$ g in $74$ $\text{cm}^{3}$, so density about $1.16$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$, higher than $1.1$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$.

D.explanation: Gives total mass $132$ g in $120$ $\text{cm}^{3}$, so density $1.1$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$ as required.

hints: Notice the starting $40$ $\text{cm}^{3}$ of glycerine of density $1.3$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$ and the unknown volume $V$ of water of density $1.0$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$.
Remember mixture density is total mass divided by total volume, with total volume $40 + V$ because volumes add.
Set $(52 + 1.0V)/(40 + V)$ equal to $1.1$ and solve for $V$ in $\text{cm}^{3}$.
walkthrough: Find the mass already present: $m = \rho V = 1.3 \times 40 = 52$ g of glycerine.
Let added water volume be $V$ $\text{cm}^{3}$. Its mass is $1.0 \times V = V$ g.
Total mass is $52 + V$ g and total volume is $40 + V$ $\text{cm}^{3}$, since volumes do not change on mixing.
Use $\rho = m/V$ for the mixture: $1.1 = (52 + V)/(40 + V)$.
Solve: $52 + V = 44 + 1.1V$, so $8 = 0.1V$ and $V = 80$ $\text{cm}^{3}$. This is option D.
